svg.title: Where the benefit of adding chemotherapy lands and what it costs: PORTEC-3 subgroups and the three directions in GOG-258
svg.desc: Schematic: where the benefit of adding chemotherapy lands and what it costs, with nothing on the figure that answers "should I have chemotherapy". The first card is a PORTEC-3 subgroup forest plot headed "the benefit is not shared out evenly". The trial enrolled 660 women at high risk with eligibility by FIGO 2009; one arm had pelvic radiotherapy 48.6 Gy and the other had chemotherapy added to the same radiotherapy, two doses of cisplatin during radiotherapy then four cycles of carboplatin plus paclitaxel, at a median follow-up of 10.1 years. Four rows are drawn on one log scale with ticks at 0.25, 0.5, 1 and 2, a black dashed line at 1, and a gold line at 0.73 marking the whole-trial row, which the other three rows are read against. First row, the whole trial at high risk, 660 women: 10-year overall survival 74.4% with chemoradiotherapy against 67.3% with radiotherapy alone, adjusted hazard ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.97, p = 0.032. Second row, FIGO 2009 stage III, 295 women: 10-year overall survival 69.5% against 56.1%, adjusted hazard ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.97, p = 0.033. Third row, serous, 105 women: 10-year overall survival 57.1% against 41.8%, adjusted hazard ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.98, p = 0.044. Fourth row, FIGO 2009 stage I to II, for which the article gives no n and so the figure gives none either: 5-year overall survival 83.8% against 82.0%, hazard ratio 0.84, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.38, p = 0.50, an interval drawn plainly crossing 1 and labelled both "95% CI crosses 1" and "a different endpoint". Beneath the card a line reads: the stage I to II row runs from 0.52 to 1.38 and crosses 1, so no benefit is visible in that group; it is also 5-year overall survival rather than the 10-year endpoint of the rows above, so the four rows can be read for direction on one ruler but cannot be added to or subtracted from one another. The second card is the price, the other row of numbers in the same trial, PORTEC-3 with 330 women in each arm; three pairs of bars share one 0 to 100 per cent scale, the upper bar of each pair being chemoradiotherapy and the lower radiotherapy alone. First pair, grade 3 or worse adverse events during treatment: 60% (198/330) against 12% (41/330), p less than 0.0001. Second pair, grade 2 or worse neuropathy at three years: 8% against 1%. Third pair, grade 2 or worse adverse events at five years: 38% against 23%, p = 0.002. Beneath the card: seven percentage points of 10-year overall survival is what that whole row of numbers buys; the figure above says the benefit is concentrated in particular groups, and this row is paid by everybody. The third card is GOG-258, asking what happens when radiotherapy is added on top of chemotherapy, where the three recurrence sites run opposite ways. It enrolled 813 women with 736 analysable, FIGO 2009 stage III or IVA; the primary endpoint was recurrence-free survival and it showed no difference, the proportion alive and free of recurrence at 60 months being 59% (53 to 65) with chemoradiotherapy against 58% (53 to 64) with chemotherapy alone, hazard ratio 0.90, 90% confidence interval 0.74 to 1.10. Below it three boxes each carry an arrow whose direction is the direction of that site. First box, vaginal recurrence, arrow pointing down for fewer in the arm that added radiotherapy: 2% with chemoradiotherapy against 7% with chemotherapy alone, hazard ratio 0.36 (0.16 to 0.82). Second box, pelvic and para-aortic nodal recurrence, arrow pointing down for fewer in the arm that added radiotherapy: 11% against 20%, hazard ratio 0.43 (0.28 to 0.66). Third box, distant recurrence, arrow pointing up for more in the arm that added radiotherapy: 27% against 21%, hazard ratio 1.36 (1.00 to 1.86), with the added label "the lower bound sits right on 1.00". Beneath the card: grade 3 to 5 adverse events were 58% with chemoradiotherapy against 63% with chemotherapy alone; and the lower bound of the interval on the distant box sits right on 1.00 and is an observation on a secondary endpoint, so it cannot be read as "radiotherapy does harm", while equally the first two boxes leave "radiotherapy is useless" with nowhere to stand. At the foot of the figure a gold-bordered panel states that this figure does not answer "should I have chemotherapy": what it draws is where the benefit lands and what it costs, and adding chemotherapy or not depends on stage and which version, histology, molecular classification, whether the nodes were staged, and whether your heart, lungs, liver and kidneys can carry that 60% rate of grade 3 or worse adverse events. The proper place for the decision is the multidisciplinary team meeting, with gynaecological oncology, medical oncology and radiation oncology having all seen your material; and PORTEC-3 and GOG-258 ask questions that run in opposite directions, with different cohorts, designs and endpoints, so the two cards must not be compared directly.
